meaning: Daughter of Dakṣa and wife of the sage Kaśyapa, mother of the Daityas, the demon race — the counterpart of her sister Aditi, who is mother of the gods.

phonemes.desc: Long ī as in “see”; the name is a-diti with the negation removed.
The feminine abstract ending; the name means “the bound one”.
The sister of Aditi — boundless — and mother of the anti-gods.

kin.label: Sister
kin.form: Aditi — the unfettered; Diti is her bound twin in name

kin.label: Sons
kin.form: the Daityas — Hiraṇyākṣa, Hiraṇyakaśipu, and the rest

pronunciation.note: The name is a mirror of her sister’s: where Aditi is “un-bound”, Diti is the “bound” — and her sons are the gods’ enemies.

domains.title: Mother of the Daityas
domains.subtitle: The Bound One, Mother of the Anti-Gods
domains.lead: Diti is the mother of the anti-gods: the Daityas, the demonic dynasty whose wars with the gods drive half the Purāṇic mythology. Daughter of Dakṣa, wife of the sage Kaśyapa, twin in name of the unfettered Aditi, she mothers the bound ones — the race of Hiraṇyākṣa and Hiraṇyakaśipu, whose boons made them nearly invincible.

mythology.lead: Diti’s mythology is her maternity: everything the Daityas do, she enables — and one thing she undoes, in the Maruts episode, where Indra’s violence against her pregnant body produces the storm-gods from the womb’s fragments. She is the anti-mother of the anti-gods, the bound one whose children strain against every bond except hers.

myths.title: The Maruts from the Broken Womb
myths.text: The oldest Diti-story has Indra hurl the vajra into her womb, shattering a hundred sons in embryo; the fragments become the Maruts, the storm-gods who yet serve Indra. Diti’s grief and the storm-gods’ loyalty are the hymn’s tension: the anti-mother’s broken children, adopted by her enemy.

myths.title: The Boon of Hiraṇyakaśipu
myths.text: Her son Hiraṇyakaśipu, devastated by his brother Hiraṇyākṣa’s death at Varāha’s tusk, won from Brahmā the boon that he could not die by day or night, indoors or out, by man or beast, on earth or sky. The boon made him lord of the three worlds — until Narasiṃha, the man-lion at dusk on a threshold, ended him. Diti’s line is the engine of the avatāra cycle.

myths.title: The Grandson Who Worshipped the Enemy
myths.text: Prahlāda, son of Hiraṇyakaśipu and thus Diti’s grandson, loved Vishnu from the womb — the devotee born in the anti-god’s house. The Purāṇas make his devotion the theology of bhakti itself: the bound dynasty’s finest fruit was the boy who could not be burned, poisoned, or thrown, for his god held him.

myths.title: Daughter of Dakṣa, Wife of Kaśyapa
myths.text: The Purāṇic theogonies make Diti one of Dakṣa’s thirteen daughters given to Kaśyapa: Aditi mothers the Ādityas, Diti the Daityas, Danu the Dānavas, and the rest of creation’s factions follow the wives. The marriage-bed of Kaśyapa is, in the genealogists’ scheme, the factory of the cosmos’s parties.

lore.syncretism: Diti is the shadow-twin of Aditi — the Purāṇic genealogists built the whole deva-asura divide from the two sisters’ names. Her line’s fate — Hiraṇyakaśipu slain, Prahlāda saved — was read by the bhakti commentators as the triumph of devotion over lineage; and modern comparative study pairs her with the bound Titans of Greek genealogy.
lore.culturalLegacy: The Prahlāda story, carried by her line, is the subcontinent’s most retold tale of devotional defiance — every schoolchild’s Sanskrit reader has it. The Daitya-vaṃśa genealogies structured the Purāṇas’ entire mythology of conflict; and the name Diti survives in modern India as a girl’s name, the bound one given with a prayer for release.
lore.extendedMeditation: Diti: the name that is Aditi with the freedom removed. Restored plainly, it stands as the lexicon’s reminder that every boundless has its bound — the anti-gods’ mother holds a name the schoolchild can spell and the theologian cannot exhaust. Two syllables, one negation, a dynasty of enemies.

sources.name: Matsya Purāṇa (Kaśyapa’s wives and the factions)

lore.archaeology: Diti has no temples — her cult is narrative. But her sons’ defeat carved the great Narasiṃha reliefs of Ellora and Mamallapuram, and the Prahlāda panels of every medieval temple tell her line’s story in stone.
lore.cult: None of her own; her ‘cult’ is the telling of her grandsons’ tales. The Holi festival’s Holikā-burning retells the Prahlāda cycle’s fire episode — the bound dynasty’s pyre, annually lit.
lore.iconography: Rarely imaged; when shown, a queen among the thirteen daughters of Dakṣa, or the wounded mother of the Purāṇic paintings. Her true icon is genealogical — the family-tree’s anti-branch.
lore.reception: Comparative mythology cites the Aditi-Diti pair as the cleanest case of name-negation structuring a pantheon’s moral geography; and the Prahlāda cycle, her line’s redemption, is the standard text of bhakti theology’s triumph over birth. She remains the study of the anti-mother: maternity without a single maternal myth of her own.
